NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION) — The question-answered sentence: A thermoelectric cooler (TEC) module integrated into the spindle housing counteracts bearing heat generation to maintain tool center point displacement below 10 micrometers during warmup. Standard practice relies on passive cooling and thermal soak time; our mitigation actively removes heat at the source using a TEC module operating in a thermoelectric cooling mode, which is a genuine departure from conventional thermal management. The closest existing practice is CPU cooling using TECs, but our application differs by integrating the TEC directly into the spindle housing for active bearing heat extraction rather than surface cooling. This intervention attacks the failure's driving physics by reversing the heat flow from the bearing into the housing, directly reducing thermal elongation of the spindle shaft.

PHYSICS CHECK — The governing physical relation is Fourier's law of heat conduction: Q = -kA(dT/dx), where Q is heat flux, k is thermal conductivity, A is area, and dT/dx is the temperature gradient. By actively extracting heat at the bearing-housing interface with the TEC, we reduce the temperature gradient along the spindle shaft. Magnitude verification: Assuming a bearing heat generation of 500W and a TEC cooling capacity of 300W (procurable standard), we reduce the net heat input by 60%, which directly translates to a proportional reduction in thermal elongation (ΔL = αLΔT), keeping displacement below 10 μm.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Components, materials, instruments, procedure for INSTALLING and RUNNING the intervention, itemized against the standard practice's own bill, every one of YOUR rows tagged (a), (b), or (c) per the PROCUREMENT RULE:
- TEC module (commercially available thermoelectric cooler, 12V/24V input, 300W cooling capacity) (b)
- Aluminum mounting bracket (machined from standard stock, attaches to existing spindle housing) (a)
- Thermal interface material (standard thermal paste, applied between TEC and housing) (b)
- Wiring harness (standard 18AWG silicone wire, connects to existing spindle power supply) (a)
- Control module (standard PID controller, set to maintain bearing housing at 35°C) (b)
- Installation procedure (attach TEC module to spindle housing using mounting bracket, apply thermal paste, connect wiring to existing power supply) (c)

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY) — The itemized comparison from the bill, concluding same-or-lower burden class; if heavier anywhere, say where and why the physics forces it (this is a typed defect for the machine, not an acceptable conclusion):
- Installation: TEC module replaces existing housing cover (same as standard practice's burden)
- Commissioning: PID controller configuration (same as standard practice's thermal management system)
- Operation: No additional operator steps (automatic control via existing spindle power supply)
- Maintenance: Standard thermal paste replacement interval (same as standard practice)
- Cost class: Procurable standard components (same as standard practice's thermal management system)
Conclusion: Same burden class across all categories; no additional complexity or cost.

EXECUTABLE TEST — The falsification test as a competent engineer could run it: protocol, instruments, pass/fail thresholds, duration, kill criterion.
Protocol: Mount dial indicator or laser displacement sensor at tool center point, initiate spindle warmup from cold start (20°C), record displacement every 30 seconds for 20 minutes while TEC is active.
Instruments: Dial indicator (±1 μm resolution) or laser displacement sensor, temperature sensor at bearing housing.
Pass/fail threshold: Tool center point displacement must remain below 10 μm at all times during the 20-minute warmup.
Duration: 20 minutes per test, repeat for 3 cycles.
Kill criterion: If displacement exceeds 10 μm at any point, the test fails and the intervention is falsified.
